3. **A bounded index designed not to silently rot.** The index loads every session and
   Claude Code reads the first 200 lines / 25 KB (documented behavior), so an unbounded index silently
   drops memories off the end. Engramory warns at 150 lines / 20 KB, compacts-or-asks
   before 200 / 25 KB, and ships a hard `PreToolUse` hook backstop (it blocks only
   *growth* past the cap — shrinking/compaction edits always pass). Both the line and
   byte caps apply — whichever is hit first triggers (an index can be under the line
   count yet over on bytes when the lines run long).

   Claude Code has since followed up on this natively: v2.1.186 (released
   2026-06-22) reminds the agent to compact the index when it nears the cap, and
   v2.1.210 (released 2026-07-14) turned an over-cap write into an explicit error
   instead of a silent truncation. Both are after-the-fact alerts, though — the
   write still lands, and entries past the cap stay invisible until someone
   compacts. Engramory's hook denies the write *before* it happens, so a write
   through the matched edit tools never leaves the index over-cap in the first
   place (writes outside them — a shell, an MCP file tool — are not gated; see the
   status note above and SKILL.md §8). The native alerts validate the direction
   and make a welcome second layer — and older versions and other hosts still
   have neither.

## How it compares

| | storage | recall | human-readable | typed ontology | curation discipline | bounded index | infra |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Engramory** | md files | loaded index → open file | ✅ | ✅ role-based (4) | ✅ contract (model-run) | ✅ 150/200 + hook | none |
| CC auto-memory | md files | loaded index → open file | ✅ | ✅ same 4 types | partial (auto) | ~200-line window* | none (built-in) |
| basic-memory | md + SQLite | semantic/FTS search | ✅ | ✅ freeform type | schema + overwrite checks | ❌ (no loaded index) | SQLite + embeddings |
| obsidian-second-brain | md vault | index-first + search | ✅ | folder-typed | ✅ reconcile/lint | partial | none |
| mem0 / Zep | vector/graph DB | semantic | ❌ (DB) | typed (prefs/episodic/proc.; Zep custom) | auto-extract | n/a | DB + embeddings |
| [agentmemory](https://github.com/rohitg00/agentmemory) | SQLite + vector index (+opt. graph) | hybrid BM25+vector (+opt. graph), RRF | ❌ (DB/engine) | ✅ 4-tier lifecycle (work./epis./sem./proc.) | auto (capture + dedup + decay) | n/a | iii engine (local) + opt. embeddings |

Engramory's lane: **minimalism + actionable role typing + curation discipline, zero
infra.** It does *not* try to out-search basic-memory, out-scale mem0, or
out-capture agentmemory — those solve a different problem (auto-capture /
auto-ingest at volume) at a different cost point. agentmemory is the closest
heavyweight foil: also local-first, but it bets on automatic capture (lifecycle
hooks) + hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vectors + optional graph) on a SQLite/`iii`
engine, where Engramory bets on hand-curation + a tiny always-loaded index and
ships no engine at all.

\* Claude Code's [memory docs](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/memory)
document this exactly: *"the first 200 lines of `MEMORY.md`, or the first 25KB,
whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation."* Other hosts
vary, so the window stays configurable via the hook's env vars.

## Where it fits — and the goal

Engramory is a **portable memory *discipline*, not a

plugins.description: Native Rapid-MLX provider for DeepSeek Harness (dsh) — dsh reads model facts from the server instead of your settings.yaml.
plugins.readme_text:
# @raullenchai/dsh-provider

A native [Rapid-MLX](https://github.com/raullenchai/Rapid-MLX) provider for
[DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) — so `dsh`
gets its model facts from the server instead of from whatever you typed into
`settings.yaml`.

[![CI](https://github.com/raullenchai/rapid-mlx-dsh-provider/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/raullenchai/rapid-mlx-dsh-provider/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

> **Status: published to npm** as
> [`@raullenchai/dsh-provider`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@raullenchai/dsh-provider).
> The end-to-end `dsh` run in [Verified](#verified) was on an M3 Ultra against
> `dsh 0.1.0-rc.7`; `dsh 0.1.0-rc.8` is API-compatible — the `LlmAdapter`
> contract is byte-identical and the only changes are additive — and the
> adapter is re-verified against rc.8 at the protocol and unit-test level.
> DSH is still a developer preview that moves fast, so treat this as tracking
> a moving target, not a frozen compatibility promise.

## What it does for you

DSH can already talk to a local Rapid-MLX server through its generic
`openai-completions` provider. That route works — but it knows nothing about
your model beyond what you hand-wrote:

```yaml
# what the generic route makes you maintain, by hand, per model
llm-pi-ai:
  providers:
    rapid-mlx:
      baseURL: http://localhost:8000/v1
      defaultContextWindow: 262144      # you looked this up. is it still right?
      models:
        - id: qwen3.6-35b-8bit
          contextWindow: 262144
          reasoningEfforts: {off: none, low: low, medium: medium, high: high}
```

Rapid-MLX's `/v1/models` already publishes all of that and more. This adapter
reads it, so:

**1. Nothing to hand-write, and nothing to re-write when you switch models.**
Swap what `rapid-mlx serve` is running and `dsh` follows. No re-running setup,
no stale numbers.

**2. The reasoning control tells the truth.** Rapid-MLX reports whether a model
actually has a reasoning parser. A model that can't reason no longer shows an
off/low/medium/high selector that does nothing.

**3. Compaction is timed with the capacity that actually fits this Mac, not a
number that drifted.** This is the one that quietly costs you.
`dsh-compaction-basic` asks the provider for the route's capacity and compacts
at `thresholdRatio × capacity` (0.8 by default). The provider prefers the
server's **`max_model_len`** — Rapid-MLX's memory-fitted ceiling (what fits in
unified memory: weights + KV cache), in the vLLM/SGLang-standard field — over
the native `context_window`, and falls back to `context_window` on an older
server that doesn't report it. So compaction is timed to what the machine can
actually hold, not the model's advertised window (which it may not have room
for) and not a hand-written number copied from another model.

## Install

Needs Node ≥ 22.15 (dsh imports Node's Zstd stream API without declaring it)
and a running Rapid-MLX server.

```sh
# From npm:
dsh plugin --profile web add @raullenchai/dsh-provider

# …or straight from source — the package ships plain JS with no build step:
dsh plugin --profile web add github:raullenchai/rapid-mlx-dsh-provider

export RAPID_MLX_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000/v1     # optional; this is the default
dsh web
```

Then point the agent at the route:

```yaml
# $DSH_HOME/settings.yaml
agent-default-model:
  provider: rapid-mlx
  model: qwen3.6-35b-8bit
```

Verified: that command installs and activates as a profile layer against
`dsh 0.1.0-rc.7`. To hack on it locally instead, see
[Local development](#local-development).

## Model management (v0.2.0)

Beyond the provider route, the plugin registers five tools and a `/rapid-mlx`
command so the agent can see and manage models without leaving the session.
The split follows which surface actually owns each fact: served-model facts
come from the structured HTTP `/v1/models`; the download cache and pull/remove
are CLI-only, so those — and only those — shell out to `rapid-mlx` through the
harness subprocess seam.

| Tool | Source | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `rapid_mlx_serving` | HTTP `/v1/models` | The model(s) served right now, deduped, with context window, reasoning/tool parsers, MoE/hybrid, and modalities. |
| `rapid_mlx_cached` | `rapid-mlx models --cached` | Downloaded models and their on-disk size. |
| `rapid_mlx_pull` | `rapid-mlx pull <name>` | Download a model (alias or HF repo id). Cancellable; no fixed deadline. |
| `rapid_mlx_remove` | `rapid-mlx rm -y <name>` | Delete a cached model to free disk. |
| `rapid_mlx_health` | HTTP + `rapid-mlx --version` | API up? CLI reachable? Reported as two independent facts. |

`/rapid-mlx` prints a one-shot overview: health, the served model and its facts,
and total cache disk usage.

The CLI is resolved from the `cliCommand` config (default `rapid-mlx` on
`PATH`, or `$RAPID_MLX_CLI`); set it to an absolute path if the binary is not on
the harness's `PATH`. `rapid_mlx_pull`/`rapid_mlx_remove` are the only tools
that change anything on disk, and they run non-interactively (`rm` is forced
with `-y` because the subprocess seam ignores stdin).

## Verified

Against `dsh 0.1.0-rc.7` on an M3 Ultra:

- Installs and **activates as a profile layer** (no "declares no `dsh.bundle`"
  warning; the entry shows up in `dsh --profile headless --dump-config`).
- Registers the `rapid-mlx` route with `ctx.llm` and serves real queries.
- Plain chat, a single tool call, and the multi-step bug-fix task that gates
  Rapid-MLX releases — the last one fixed the bug and made the target repo's own
  test pass, verified independently, in 36 s on `qwen3.6-35b-8bit`.

## Not done yet

Being explicit, because the point of the adapter is to *use* what the server
says and some of it is still only read:

- `recommended_sampling` — should be applied automatically per model.
- `tool_call_parser` — should let `dsh` fail fast on a model that cannot emit
  `tool_calls`, instead of looping.
- `is_hybrid` / `is_moe` / `capabilities` — read, not yet acted on.
- **Memory-aware capacity.** Today `resolveModel()` reports the model's
  *advertised* context window. On a Mac the real ceiling is unified memory, and
  reporting that instead is the biggest remaining win — it needs Rapid-MLX to
  expose a usable-capacity figure first.
- Images are not carried through `stream()` — but they now **refuse** with
  `LlmError(..., 'UNSUPPORTED')` rather than being dropped, per the cookbook.
  Text, reasoning and tool calls are carried.
- The route is registered as `rapid-mlx`. If your `settings.yaml` also declares
  a `rapid-mlx` provider under `llm-pi-ai`, the two compete for one route name
  (`registerAdapter` owns provider exclusivity). Use one or rename ours.

## Conformance with the official adapter contract

Built against
[`docs/cookbook/adding-an-llm-adapter.md`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/main/docs/cookbook/adding-an-llm-adapter.md)
and its "protocol obligations" section. Each item has a test:

| Obligation | How it is met |
|---|---|
| `usage` before `finish`, nothing after `finish` | usage is buffered and flushed at end-of-stream, so a trailing usage-only chunk cannot reorder it |
| Tool-call `arguments` are raw JSON strings end to end | fragments stream as `argumentsDelta` and reassemble unparsed |
| Block indexes in first-seen order, reused per block | verified across a reasoning-then-text response |
| Errors take exactly two sanctioned paths | transport/protocol failures **throw** `LlmError` with a stable code; nothing ends the stream quietly |
| Honor `options.signal` | passed to `fetch` and to the SSE reader; an `AbortError` is re-thrown unchanged, not reclassified |
| A field the provider cannot honor throws `UNSUPPORTED` | image content refuses instead of being narrowed away |
| Config is a schemastery schema with env fallback | `export const Config`, fed from `cordis.patch.yml` via `!!js process.env.RAPID_MLX_BASE_URL` |

`finish.replayState` is not emitted: Rapid-MLX needs no native response ids
or signatures on follow-up calls, so there is nothing lossless to project.

## Three things worth knowing before you edit this

Each of these cost real

plugins.description: Runtime evidence that helps agents trace, profile, and burn down hotspots in application and native code, GPU kernels, and inference stacks.
plugins.readme_text:
flameox

Bounded local runtime evidence for coding agents.

Flameox coordinates profilers, benchmark tools, trace processors, and direct local targets. It turns an explicit artifact or command into bounded evidence while keeping durable preservation optional. The agent chooses hypotheses and experiments; Flameox records observed inputs, execution provenance, typed evidence, coverage, and limitations. There is no workspace to initialize or project configuration to maintain. Pass exact artifact paths to analysis and an explicit argv plus absolute working directory to capture. Flameox does not search parent directories, edit project files, or provide a hosted service. ## Quick start Configure an MCP client with the global setup command: ```console npx flameox@latest setup ``` Setup detects supported clients and asks which configurations to update. For automation, select clients explicitly, for example `--client codex --yes` or `--all --yes`; `--dry-run` reports the paths and actions without writing. Setup preserves unrelated client configuration and does not change project files. See [the npm package guide](npm/README.md) for details. Update existing MCP registrations with: ```console npx flameox@latest update ``` `update --check` reports available updates without changing configuration. Updates preserve each client's provider extras and settings, verify the new environment before changing release pins, and report which clients need a restart or reconnect. Use `--client codex` to select one client, or `--version 0.2.8` to select a specific release, including for rollback. The Python CLI exposes the same `flameox update` command. For direct CLI use, pass exact artifact paths or an explicit command: ```console uvx flameox analyze preview_artifact /absolute/path/to/artifact.json uvx flameox capture --provider direct --cwd "$PWD" -- python benchmark.py ``` To launch the stdio MCP server manually: ```console uvx flameox mcp serve ``` For local development, clone the repository, install its development dependencies, and inspect the available tools: ```console git clone https://github.com/morluto/flameox.git cd flameox uv sync --extra dev --extra memory --extra trace --extra cpu uv run flameox mcp inspect ``` ## Evidence and storage Analysis and unpreserved capture use bounded session scratch. Session `analysis_id` values expire when evicted or when the server stops. Explicit preservation creates the user-level Flameox data directory and stores native bytes and a canonical evidence bundle by SHA-256. Set `FLAMEOX_DATA_DIR` to choose another location. Preservation is optional; it does not imply full console-output retention. Flameox distinguishes observed, derived, and inferred claims. Profiles guide exploration but do not establish causality or performance improvement. Confirmatory claims require representative workloads, declared metrics and estimands, compatible identities, preserved samples, and a semantic oracle. ## MCP The MCP server has no workspace binding. It exposes named analysis and capture tools through the same operation registry as the CLI. Analysis tools accept explicit sources; capture tools accept a typed target and provider. Tool schemas expose operation-specific fields directly. Inspect the catalog with `flameox mcp inspect`; use `--tool TOOL_NAME` for focused schemas and examples. The complete contract and current tool catalog are in [the interface guide](docs/interfaces.md). Tools return their full bounded results inline, including failures and recovery actions. Preserved evidence has a durable `evidence_id`; `inspect_evidence` returns its redacted metadata and replay sources inline. Capture takes argv, not a shell string. A direct target supplies an absolute working directory and bounded environment overrides. Results may include `next_page`; replay its named analysis tool and arguments unchanged. Capture continuations read collected artifacts and do not rerun the target. MCP work belongs to the live request, so cancellation applies directly and no detached job survives a restart. ## Documentation - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) describes process and package boundaries. - [Storage and evidence](docs/storage-and-evidence.md) defines preservation and provenance. - [Investigations](docs/investigations.md) covers experiments, comparison, and evidence quality. - [Adapters](docs/adapters.md) documents provider compatibility and integration policy. - [Runtime safety](docs/runtime-safety.md) covers limits, recovery, integrity, and privacy. - [Interfaces](docs/interfaces.md) defines CLI and MCP contracts. - [Testing](docs/testing.md) describes test selections and known proof gaps. ## Development Flameox requires Python 3.12 or newer and uses the committed `uv.lock`. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup and contribution guidance. ```console uv run ruff check src tests tools uv run ruff format --check src tests tools uv run mypy src tests tools uv run pytest -q ``` Flameox is licensed under the MIT License.

plugins.description: DSH plugin: enable permessage-deflate on the WebSocket transport (/api/remote.mux) without modifying the DSH install tree
plugins.readme_text:
# dsh-ws-deflate

**English** | [简体中文](./README.zh-CN.md)

Turns on `permessage-deflate` for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (`dsh`) web's WebSocket transport, **without modifying the DSH installation**. Measured on one machine: a session transcript that left the server as **1,206,822 B went out as 350,599 B — 70.9 % fewer wire bytes**.

It is a **runtime monkey-patch, not a supported extension point.** Read "Should I install this" before installing it.

## Should I install this?

**Install it if** you open `dsh web` from somewhere that is not your own machine — a Tailscale/VPN link, a reverse proxy over the internet, any path with real latency or packet loss. DSH replays the whole session transcript over `/api/remote.mux` on every reconnect, so on a lossy link those bytes are paid repeatedly.

**Do not install it if** you only ever use `dsh web` on `localhost` or a LAN. The saving is real but you don't need it there, and what you'd be taking on in exchange is a patch against another project's internals that can go quietly stale on every upgrade.

What it costs, measured on a Windows 10 / node v24 box: **+10 ms** to `dsh` startup (alternating 4-run measurement), and zlib level 6 at **42.7 ms per 1.53 MB** of transcript. The compression is per-message above a 1 KiB threshold, so small events are untouched.

## What it actually changes

Nothing on disk. `ws@8.22.0`, `@deepseek-ai/dsh-api-gateway`, and `@deepseek-ai/dsh/lib` were compared file-by-file (sha256) against the pristine registry tarballs: **63 files, 0 mismatches, 0 extra, 0 missing**, and 0 files in the install tree written or created that day.

What it does change is one method, in memory, in the `dsh` process:

```
BEFORE  WebSocketServer.prototype.handleUpgrade = handleUpgrade(req, socket, head, cb) {   ← ws's own
AFTER   WebSocketServer.prototype.handleUpgrade = function (req, socket, head, cb) { try {  ← the wrapper
disk sha256 of ws/lib/websocket-server.js: 6d8dd89a841748c8 -> 6d8dd89a841748c8            ← unchanged
```

The wrapper sets `this.options.perMessageDeflate` at **handshake** time, which works because ws 8.x reads that option inside `handleUpgrade` (`websocket-server.js:299`/`:303`), not at construction — so it reaches the gateway's already-built `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })` (`dsh-api-gateway/lib/index.js:179`). It only opts in when nothing else set the option, so **if DSH enables compression itself upstream, this plugin steps aside automatically.**

Why the option can't just be configured: DSH exposes no key for it. The webserver's `compression` is HTTP gzip and does not cover streams.

## Install

```bash
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-ws-deflate
```

Then restart `dsh web`. The bundle list is read at startup, so no restart means no effect.

## Verify

```bash
grep 'dsh-ws-deflate' <wherever your dsh web logs>
```

You want three things:

```
[dsh-ws-deflate] permessage-deflate enabled -> …/node_modules/ws [ws 8.22.0] via path (level 6, threshold 1024 B, noContextTakeover on)
[dsh-ws-deflate] self test OK: this process negotiates permessage-deflate
[dsh-ws-deflate] negotiated permessage-deflate with Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7) …
```

The **self test** is the interesting one. DSH's browser auth rejects non-browser handshakes, so you cannot probe a live server from a script — the plugin instead builds its own `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })` on an ephemeral loopback port and does a real handshake against it. That proves *this process, with this ws copy, negotiates*, which is the claim no external probe can reach. The `negotiated …` lines then log the first few real browser handshakes (user agent truncated, `maxLog` caps it at 5, `0` disables).

Browser side, if you want it: DevTools → Network → the `remote.mux` request → Response Headers should contain `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions: permessage-deflate; …`.

## Uninstall

```bash
dsh plugin --profile web remove dsh-ws-deflate
```

Restart. Nothing needs restoring, because nothing on disk was ever different.

## Configuration

Add or edit the entry in your profile's `cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- id: ws-deflate
  name: dsh-ws-deflate
  config:
    enabled: true
    level: 6
    thresholdBytes: 1024
    noContextTakeover: true
    concurrencyLimit: 10
    selfTest: true
    maxLog: 5
```

| key | default | notes |
|---|---:|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | `false` keeps the wrapper installed but opts no handshake in |
| `level` | `6` | measured here: level 6 → ratio 0.176, level 1 → 0.238 on the same payload, at 42.7 ms vs 5.9 ms per 1.53 MB |
| `thresholdBytes` | `1024` | below this, frames go out raw (the median DSH event is ~800 B) |
| `noContextTakeover` | `true` | independent deflate stream per frame: bounded memory, and a dropped frame cannot corrupt later messages. Costs ratio, buys robustness on a lossy link — which is the whole reason to run this plugin |
| `concurrencyLimit` | `10` | cap on simultaneous compress operations |
| `selfTest` | `true` | run the loopback handshake at activation. Not hot-reloadable |
| `maxLog` | `5` | how many successful negotiations to log; `0` is silent |

Everything except `selfTest` is `.volatile()`, so editing the patch and letting the profile hot-reload re-applies it without a restart.

## How it finds the gateway's `ws` copy

A plugin cannot `import 'ws'` and get the gateway's copy. The profile is a pnpm tree that contains no `ws` at all; declaring it as a dependency installs a **second** copy — a different class object, and patching it does nothing. Three routes, tried in this order, all tested:

1. **Ask the process.** The gateway's `ws` is in the CommonJS module cache; the class found there is provably the one the gateway uses (`cached === path-required: true`). Match on `ws/lib/websocket-server.js`, **not** `ws/index.js` — ws routes `import` to `wrapper.mjs`, which goes straight at the lib file, so `index.js` never enters the cache in an ESM host. Note `lib/websocket-server.js` does `module.exports = WebSocketServer`, so the export *is* the class.
2. **Guess the path.** Honours `$DSH_HOME` (precedence: configured path > `$DSH_HOME` > `~/.dsh`) and checks `<home>/profiles/node_modules/ws`, which dsh itself creates as a junction into the install tree — the most portable entry. Plus npm-global prefixes for Windows (`%APPDATA%\npm`), Linux (`/usr/local`, `/usr/lib`) and both macOS locations (`/usr/local`, `/opt/homebrew`).
3. **Retry for ~2 s.** If neither finds anything, retry every 250 ms (unref'd, so it can never hold the process open). This is what covers an install whose prefix is not in the list: by the time the gateway has loaded, route 1 works. Tested by neutralising every candidate (`DSH_HOME` + `APPDATA` + `argv[1]` pointed at empty dirs), activating — nothing patched — then loading the gateway late: `located ws on deferred attempt 2 … via require.cache`, self test OK.

### One thing that will confuse you, on purpose

`import 'dsh-ws-deflate'` from a plain `node` script **fails** with `Cannot find package '@deepseek-ai/schemastery'`, even though the plugin loads fine inside `dsh`. That is not a bug to fix: dsh runs its own interception resolver (`dsh-app-boot/lib/index.js:1459` `scope === "installation"`, `:1479` `readPeerNames(...).has(name)`) and supplies declared peers from the installation tree. A fresh profile has no `schemastery` anywhere in it — verified on two platforms — and the plugin still activates. **So don't "verify" this plugin by importing it from a script; verify it by restarting `dsh web` and reading the log.**

## Tested on

| platform | node | dsh | ws | pnpm | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Windows 10 | v24.20.0 | 0.2.0-rc.2 | 8.22.0 | 10.18.2 | live, 3 browser handshakes logged incl. macOS Safari |
| Linux | v22.19.0 | 0.2.0-rc.2 | 8.22.0 | 12.11.2 | clean-room: fresh profile from the shipped template, installed from a packed tarball, booted on :3099, self test OK |

Both were installed from a local tarball, not from the registry. One combination per platform — treat anything else as untested. The structural guard is `typeof WebSocketServer.prototype.handleUpgrad

plugins.readme_text:
# Session Switcher

English overview below · 完整详细文档为简体中文，见 [中文说明](#中文说明)

Session Switcher (`dsh-session-switcher`) is a plugin for **DSH Desktop** that brings hold-to-switch navigation to your recently viewed sessions. Hold `Ctrl` and tap `Tab` to open a floating list of recent sessions with the next target highlighted; tap `Tab` again to move down, then release the modifier(s) to open the highlighted session (`Ctrl+Shift+Tab` moves backwards and `Esc` cancels). The highlight moves while the modifier is held, so you can skip past sessions before committing on release. It is built for DSH Desktop: in a browser tab `Ctrl+Tab` belongs to the browser, so the plugin won't fire there.

| Keys | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Hold `Ctrl`, tap `Tab` | Open the list and highlight the next recently viewed session; tap again to move down |
| `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `Tab` | Move the highlight backwards |
| Release the modifier(s) | Open the highlighted session and close the list |
| `Esc` | Cancel without switching |
| `Enter` / click a row | Open that session immediately |
| `↑` / `↓` | Move the highlight while the list is open |
| Click outside / window blur | Cancel |

## 安装 / Installation

### 从插件管理器安装（推荐）/ Install from the plugin manager

The plugin is a normal DSH bundle, so DSH's own plugin manager can install and enable it:

1. Open the **Plugins** page in DSH (the plugin manager page in the sidebar; 中文界面为「插件」).
2. Select **Add plugin** → **Install a third-party plugin**（「添加插件」→「安装第三方插件」）.
3. Enter the repository address and select **Install**:

   ```text
   https://github.com/Yporcupine/dsh-session-switcher
   ```

4. If DSH asks for a restart, restart DSH Desktop. The installer adds the dependency to your profile and enables the bundle for you; no manual configuration is needed.

To disable or uninstall the plugin later, use the same **Plugins** page.

### 命令行安装 / Install with the CLI

The same installation is available from the `dsh` CLI:

```bash
dsh plugin add https://github.com/Yporcupine/dsh-session-switcher
```

Use `--profile <name>` to target a specific profile (for example `dsh plugin --profile desktop add ...`). The CLI may ask you to restart DSH afterwards. You can also install the release tarball — paste the download link of the `dsh-session-switcher-1.3.0.tgz` asset from the [Releases page](https://github.com/Yporcupine/dsh-session-switcher/releases) into the same dialog or command.

### 本地开发安装 / Local checkout (development)

To hack on the plugin, run a checkout as a linked bundle. Prefer DSH's own installer — it writes the `link:` dependency **and** runs the profile's package install, so the checkout is linked into the profile; editing the manifest by hand alone skips that step and the bundle is skipped at startup.

1. Clone the repository into your DSH bundles directory (`~/.dsh/bundles/`; Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dsh\bundles\`):

   ```bash
   # macOS / Linux
   git clone https://github.com/Yporcupine/dsh-session-switcher.git ~/.dsh/bundles/session-switcher
   ```

   ```powershell
   # Windows (PowerShell)
   git clone https://github.com/Yporcupine/dsh-session-switcher.git "$env:USERPROFILE\.dsh\bundles\session-switcher"
   ```

2. Install the checkout through the same add-plugin flow, pointing it at the local directory: **Plugins** page → **Add plugin** → **Install a third-party plugin** → enter the absolute path of the checkout (`/home/<you>/.dsh/bundles/session-switcher`, `/Users/<you>/.dsh/bundles/session-switcher`, or `C:/Users/<you>/.dsh/bundles/session-switcher`). Or use the CLI:

   ```bash
   dsh plugin --profile desktop add /home/<you>/.dsh/bundles/session-switcher
   ```

   DSH records a `link:` dependency, installs it into the profile, and enables the bundle.

3. Restart DSH Desktop. After later edits to the checkout, restart DSH Desktop (or disable and re-enable the bundle on the **Plugins** page) to remount the client module.

#### 手动回退 / Fallback: edit the profile manifest by hand

Only if the installer cannot be used. Edit the DSH Desktop profile manifest, `~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/package.json` (Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dsh\profiles\desktop\package.json`), to add the dependency and the bundle selection:

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "dsh-session-switcher": "link:/home/<you>/.dsh/bundles/session-switcher"
  },
  "dsh": {
    "profile": {
      "bundles": ["...", "dsh-session-switcher"]
    }
  }
}
```

Use the absolute path of your clone: `/home/<you>/...` on Linux, `/Users/<you>/...` on macOS, `C:/Users/<you>/...` on Windows (JSON paths use forward slashes on every OS); from the profile directory the relative form `link:../../bundles/session-switcher` resolves to the same location. Then relink and reinstall the profile — without this the linked package never reaches `node_modules` and the bundle is skipped:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile desktop install
```

Restart DSH Desktop afterwards.

> **浏览器 / Browser:** the shortcuts target DSH Desktop. In a browser tab `Ctrl+Tab` belongs to the browser, so the plugin won't fire there.

## 中文说明

DSH Desktop 插件：按住 `Ctrl` 敲 `Tab`，弹出「最近会话」浮动小窗，高亮待切换的会话；
**松开修饰键即打开高亮会话**并收起小窗。

| 操作 | 效果 |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Tab`（按住 Ctrl 连按 Tab） | 打开浮动窗，高亮「下一个最近查看的会话」；继续按 Tab 依次下移 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Tab` | 反向移动高亮 |
| 松开修饰键 | 打开高亮会话，关闭小窗 |
| `Esc` | 取消，不切换 |
| `Enter` / 鼠标点击某一行 | 立即打开该会话 |
| `↑` / `↓` | 移动高亮（小窗打开时） |
| 点击小窗外 / 窗口失焦 | 取消 |

- 插件按 DSH Desktop 设计：浏览器里 `Ctrl+Tab` 归浏览器所有，插件不会被触发。
- macOS 同样使用 `Ctrl+Tab` / `Ctrl+Shift+Tab`（`Cmd+Tab` 是系统应用切换，应用收不到）。

### 实现要点：为什么用 fixed 输入而不是可编辑快捷键

DSH Desktop 的**原生键盘桥**会先于页面拦截「可编辑快捷键」的按键组合，然后 Electron
会吞掉随后的**修饰键 keyup**（DSH 官方 shortcuts 文档的 “Understand the implementation” 一节
也说明：Electron 在原生拦截之后可能省略 keyup）。一旦 `Ctrl` 的 keyup 到不了页面，浮动窗就无法知道「Ctrl 已松开」，
只能等下一次按键——这正是早期版本「松开 Ctrl 无反应、要再按一次 Ctrl 才切换」的根因
（已用合成按键 + UI Automation 实测复现：`Ctrl+Tab`、`Ctrl+B` 等任何可编辑快捷键之后
都收不到 `keyup`）。

因此 `Ctrl+Tab` / `Ctrl+Shift+Tab` 注册为 **fixed 输入动作**（`ctx.shortcuts.registerFixed`
+ `ctx.shortcuts.observeFixedInput`）：fixed 动作不走原生桥拦截，留在正常的 DOM 输入路径，
修饰键 keyup 可以正常收到，于是「松手提交」可靠。代价是这两行在
**Settings → Keyboard shortcuts**（`Mod+/`）里显示为只读条目（Application 分组，键帽
`Ctrl + Tab` / `Ctrl + Shift + Tab`），不能改键；不想要时停用/卸载插件即可。

#### 为什么点击行曾「只关窗、不切换」（已修复）

DSH 的 shortcuts 服务在**每个 `pointerdown`** 上都会给 fixed 输入观察者发一次
`{ type: "reset" }`（用于中断多键序列）。早期版本把 reset 一律当作取消：鼠标按下瞬间
小窗就被卸载，行的 React `click` 永远来不及触发——于是「点一下小窗消失，但会话没切换」。
现在的做法是：在 **window 捕获阶段**（早于 shortcuts 服务的 document 捕获 reset）先判断
这次按下是否落在小窗内；**落在窗内的按下不算取消**，只吞掉紧接着的 reset，让行正常收到
click 并切换；点到窗外仍然立即取消。松开指针（`pointerup`/`pointercancel`）后恢复常规
reset 行为。

### 参考实现

当前 ChatGPT / Codex 桌面端（2026，版本 26）把 `Ctrl+Tab` 定义为 **“Next recently viewed chat”**，
`Ctrl+Shift+Tab` 为 **“Previous recently viewed chat”**（另有 `Ctrl+PageDown/PageUp`、
`Ctrl+Shift+]`/`[` 等别名）；Codex 应用更新日志也提到加入了「跳转到最近线程的键盘快捷键」。
本插件按这个语义实现：

- 列表 = **最近查看顺序（MRU）**：当前会话 → 查看历史（最近查看的在前）→ 其余会话按侧边栏
  最近更新排序；每次查看会话都会更新查看历史；
- 按住修饰键时只移动高亮，**松开才切换**（VS Code / Alt-Tab 式 hold-modifier switcher）；
- 列表跳过已归档会话和子代理（subagent）会话；当前未开始的新会话排在最前。

参考链接：

- <https://defkey.com/chatgpt-windows-app-2026-shortcuts>（ChatGPT Windows App 26.x 快捷键表）
- <https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog?type=codex-app>（Codex app 更新日志）

### 样式

面板沿用 DSH 菜单样式：`--dsw-specific-menu` 表面、`--dsw-elevation-prominent` 阴影、
`--dsw-radius-xl` 圆角、`--dsw-alias-state-business-primary` 选中强调色，跟随明暗主题；
行内显示会话标题、所属工作区与相对时间，当前会话带「当前」标记。

某一行的会话**正在运行**（active turn）时，行右侧显示一个 14px 的旋转圆圈，复用 DSH
侧边栏 `StateDot` 的 ongoing 外观：1.5s 线性旋转 + 1.5s 虚线弧动画，描边继承
`--dsw-alias-label-tertiary`；`prefers-reduced-motion` 下两段动画停止、弧固定。运行状态
来自 frame 槽作用域提供的 `useSessionStatus` 钩子（实时订阅），取不到时回退到会话列表
快照里的 `running` 提示；它会和「当前」标记并排显示，但始终位于最右侧。

### 文件

| 文件 | 作用 |
| --- | --- |
| `package.json` | 包清单：`dsh.bundle.patch` 声明 bundle 补丁，`dsh.client` 声明浏览器半体 |
| `cordis.patch.yml` | 向 profile 配置树插入 Host 行 `session-switcher` |
| `index.js` | Host 半体（无需挂载任何服务，空 `apply`） |
| `client.js` | 浏览器半体：fixed 输入动作 + `shell.overlay` 浮动窗 + 页面级 keyup/keydown 负责「松手提交 / Esc 取消」，并订阅会话列表维护最近查看顺序；window 捕获阶段区分「点中面板」与「点外取消」；运行中的会话行右侧渲染 `useSessionStatus` 旋转圆圈；内置中英文运行时文案 |
| `locale/*.json` | 插件市场/设置页里的标题与描述（中英文） |
| `icon.svg` | 插件图标 |
| `verify-client.cjs` | 本地校验脚本（不参与运行时）：用桩 React/DOM/服务执行真实 `client

plugins.description: TypeSafe Jev for DeepSeek Harness, the Model Context Protocol, and plain Node: typed judgments instead of prose, offline by default.
plugins.readme_text:
# jevcore
[![dshfind](https://dshfind.com/api/badge/PerryLink/jevcore?metric=downloads)](https://dshfind.com/plugins/PerryLink/jevcore?ref=badge)

[![DSH Market](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/2BingLing/dsh-market/master/assets/readme/badge-listed-en.svg)](https://dsh.market/)
[![OpenSSF Scorecard](https://api.securityscorecards.dev/projects/github.com/PerryLink/jevcore/badge)](https://api.securityscorecards.dev/projects/github.com/PerryLink/jevcore)
[![jevcore MCP server](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/PerryLink/jevcore/badges/score.svg)](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/PerryLink/jevcore)

TypeSafe [Jev](https://typesafe.ai) for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness)
and any other MCP host.

Jev is not a chat model. It answers typed questions — `noul` (yes/no), `choice`, `score` — and returns
calibrated probabilities. It does not write prose, and asking it to is a category error. This project
gives an agent exactly that surface, and nothing more.

**Offline by default. Egress disclosed. Nothing default-on.**

---

**📖 Ecosystem knowledge base** — measured data, not marketing: [plugin development guide · plugin-selection data · maintenance criteria](https://perrylink.github.io/dsh-plugin-guide/).

<!-- star-cta -->
## ⭐ 如果它帮到了你

这个插件是 [DSH 插件家族](https://github.com/PerryLink)的一员（40+ 个，全部 Apache-2.0）。如果你在用，**给个 star** —— 它不会解锁任何功能，但会让下一个人在搜索里更容易找到它。

*English:* part of a 40+ plugin family for DeepSeek Harness. If it is useful, **a star helps the next person find it** — nothing is gated behind it.


## Three packages, one decision layer

| Package | What it is | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| [`jevcore`](packages/core) | The decisions. Imports nothing from DeepSeek Harness or Cordis. | You want Jev in a plain script, a service, or your own harness |
| [`jevcore-dsh`](packages/dsh) | The DSH plugin: one service, three tools, two opt-in gates | You are running DeepSeek Harness |
| [`jevcore-mcp`](packages/mcp) | The same three tools over MCP, with a stdio binary | Your host speaks MCP but is not DSH |

The adapters are thin on purpose. `packages/dsh` is four files: it declares tool schemas and
translates hook payloads. Everything decision-shaped — the primitives, the providers, the egress
contract, the policy, the gates — lives in core, so a new adapter cannot drift from the guarantees
the others make.
One runtime requirement differs across the three: `jevcore-dsh` tracks the harness and needs
Node `^22.19.0 || >=24.0.0`, while `jevcore` and `jevcore-mcp` need `>=20`.

---

## Why this exists

Between 2026-09-17 and 09-20, nineteen plugins appeared that wire Jev into DSH. Auditing their source
found a consistent pattern: the module labelled *guard*, *gate*, or *warden* was also the module
shipping prompts, tool arguments, and file contents to a third party, and the README generally did not
say so. Several were enabled by default. One gate could be reconfigured by the model it was guarding.

This project is the same idea with those failure modes designed out:

| Property | How it is guaranteed here |
|---|---|
| No network call unless you ask for one | Default provider is an offline mock; the live path needs both `provider: live` and a resolved credential |
| Every transmission named before it happens | One startup log line per feature: `off` or `SENDS <feature> { fields }` |
| Gates register nothing when disabled | Verified by test, not by policy — a disabled gate adds no event listener at all |
| The model cannot widen its own constraints | No tool exposes gate configuration |
| A judge that cannot answer never means "allow" | Undecided resolves through explicit config, defaulting to `ask` |

---

## The egress contract

This is the part worth reading before installing.

Transmission is decided per feature, and every feature defaults to off. The plugin prints its own
contract at load:

```
[jevcore] provider=mock  endpoint=none  egress=OFF  (no network calls will be made; every answer is synthetic)
[jevcore] ready - provider=mock - gates: safety=off context=off
```

With `provider: live` and every feature enabled, the same report becomes explicit about what leaves:

```
[jevcore] provider=live  endpoint=https://api.typesafe.ai  egress=ON
[jevcore]   SENDS  tool:jev_ask  { state<=16000c questions<=4000c }
[jevcore]   SENDS  tool:jev_rank  { state<=16000c questions<=4000c }
[jevcore]   SENDS  tool:jev_check  { state<=16000c questions<=4000c }
[jevcore]   SENDS  gate:safety  { state<=8000c questions<=2000c }
[jevcore]   SENDS  gate:context  { state<=6000c questions<=2000c }
[jevcore]   redaction is best-effort; it removes named fields and known secret shapes, and cannot
             recognise an unrecognised secret in free text
```

| Feature | Off by default? | What it sends |
|---|---|---|
| `tool:jev_ask` | runs when the model calls it | the arguments the model passed, after redaction |
| `tool:jev_rank` | runs when the model calls it | the query plus every candidate |
| `tool:jev_check` | runs when the model calls it | the claim and its evidence |
| `gate:safety` | **yes — explicit opt-in** | the tool name, its arguments, the workspace root |
| `gate:context` | **yes — explicit opt-in** | a large tool result the agent just received |

The tools transmit only when the model chooses to call them, which is visible in the transcript. The
gates would run on every matching tool call, which is not, so they are opt-in.

### Redaction, and its honest limit

Before anything is sent, `src/redact.ts` runs two passes: values under sensitive field names
(`password`, `token`, `apiKey`, `authorization`, …) are replaced wholesale, and secret-shaped strings
that survive into free text are pattern-matched (`Bearer …`, `sk-…`, `ts_live_…`, AWS/GitHub/Google
key shapes, JWTs, private-key headers, credentials in connection strings).

This is a mitigation, not a permission. A secret that sits under an unrecognised key name *and* does
not match a known shape will pass through. If that possibility is unacceptable for your workload, do
not enable the live provider.

---

## Install

### As a DeepSeek Harness plugin

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add jevcore-dsh
```

Or from a checkout:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add /absolute/path/to/jevcore/packages/dsh
```

`packages/dsh` imports `jevcore` by name, so a checkout also needs core
resolvable from the profile (`add /absolute/path/to/jevcore/packages/core`).

Then confirm the row activated — the plugin list should show `jev` as `active`,
not `failed` — and check the startup report in the log.

### As an MCP server

For a host that speaks MCP, the same three tools are available over stdio:

```sh
npx -y jevcore-mcp
```

To wire it into DeepSeek Harness specifically, install a configuration-only bundle
whose patch inserts the harness's own MCP client:

```yml
- insert:
    - id: jev-mcp
      name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client'
      config:
        serverName: jev
        transport: stdio
        command: npx
        args: ['-y', 'jevcore-mcp']
        env:
          TYPESAFE_API_KEY: '<the key>'
        failOnStartupError: true
```

The env map is not optional: DSH strips every credential-shaped name — anything
containing KEY, PASSWORD, SECRET or TOKEN, in any case — from the environment it
hands a spawned server, then merges this map back in afterwards. A key exported in
your shell never arrives, and the server stays on the offline mock without
reporting an error.

The provider is chosen from the environment:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` | Selects the TypeSafe route when present |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Selects the OpenRouter route when present and no TypeSafe key is set |
| `JEV_PROVIDER` | `mock`, `live`, or `openrouter` — overrides the heuristic above |
| `TYPESAFE_MODEL` / `OPENROUTER_MODEL` | Model id for the selected route |
| `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` / `OPENROUTER_BASE_URL` | API root for the selected route |

With neither key it stays on the offline mock. Unlike the plugin, the MCP server
resolves its credential once at startup, so a missing key with
`JEV_PROVIDER=live` is a startup error rather than a per-call surprise.

plugins.description: Unofficial visual control panel and MCP bridge for DeepSeek Harness: model, workspace and permission controls, task monitoring, and reusable sessions.
plugins.readme_text:
# dsh-mcp-bridge

English | [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md)

**A visible control panel for Claude Code and Codex delegation to DeepSeek Harness.** Choose the model, provider, workspace, and new-session permissions in Harness; inspect task state through MCP; find and continue the resulting conversations.

This project is for people who want to spend less of their main model's effort on bounded supporting tasks, and make repeated Harness calls and the resulting sessions easier to manage.

> Third-party, unofficial integration. Not affiliated with or endorsed by DeepSeek, Anthropic, or OpenAI. Harness interfaces and MCP clients can change; check the compatibility notes before upgrading.

> **Archive-only maintenance in 0.2.4:** permanent deletion is disabled in every plugin entry point. The compatible `autoCleanupDays` setting now archives eligible MCP-created sessions, keeps their files, and uses the official non-stopping option; `0` turns automatic archival off. Old pending-delete files are retained unchanged and never executed. See [maintenance boundaries and upgrade notes](docs/troubleshooting.md#cleanup-limitation-and-pending-deletions).

## Why this bridge?

- **Delegate selectively.** Send a narrow review, summary, documentation task, or investigation to Harness, then bring the result back to your main agent.
- **Keep responsibility clear.** The main agent still scopes the task, checks the result, and integrates useful work.
- **Keep controls visible.** Use Harness's toolbar for task constraints and its conversations for context; use MCP status/results to inspect execution rather than relying on a silent handoff.
- **Manage repeated delegation.** Find task IDs after a disconnect, continue managed sessions, and archive conversations you want to keep.

Delegation can reduce the amount of work the main model performs, but it does not guarantee a fixed quota reduction, lower total cost, or faster completion. DeepSeek or your chosen provider can still charge for delegated work, and coordination, retries, and review still consume resources. See [choosing and measuring delegated tasks](docs/delegation.md).

## How it fits together

1. Claude Code, Codex, or another compatible MCP client sends a tool request.
2. The local bridge connects that request to the plugin running in DeepSeek Harness.
3. A Harness agent uses the configured provider, workspace, and execution permissions.
4. The client receives the task result for review and further work.

**A local bridge does not mean local model inference.** Prompts and relevant workspace content may be sent to the provider configured in Harness. Check your provider's terms and your own data-sharing permissions before delegating private material.

The current plugin installs into the **desktop profile**, so that Harness host must be running. This is a good fit if you already use Harness and delegate frequently. A one-off task may not justify the extra installation and process. Harness also has an official CLI; other hosting profiles for this plugin have not been verified. [CLI and hosting FAQ](docs/troubleshooting.md#does-harness-have-a-cli).

## Quick start

Bridge version: **0.2.4**. Target Harness desktop version: **0.2.1-rc.2**. Build with Node.js **22+** and npm. Maintainer-provided verification notes cover Windows; they do not establish support for every platform or MCP client.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/FishCityBee/dsh-mcp-bridge.git
cd dsh-mcp-bridge
npm ci
npm run build
```

Install `dist-package/` with Harness's bundled CLI. Windows PowerShell example, with paths replaced for your installation:

```powershell
& "D:\Program Files\Deepseek Harness\resources\runtime\cli\bin\dsh.cmd" plugin --profile desktop add "C:\path\to\dsh-mcp-bridge\dist-package"
```

Completely quit Harness, including the tray process, and reopen it. In the bridge toolbar, select your provider/model, a disposable default workspace, and read-only new-session permissions. Automatic archival defaults to off; enable it only after reviewing its scope.

Register the relay in the client you use, with its absolute path:

```sh
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope user dsh-harness -- node "C:/path/to/dsh-mcp-bridge/dist-package/bin/stdio.mjs"

# Codex
codex mcp add dsh-harness -- node "C:/path/to/dsh-mcp-bridge/dist-package/bin/stdio.mjs"
```

Ask the client to call `harness_status`, `list_models`, and `list_workspaces` before starting a task. Then try one small task with no file changes. Model tasks can incur provider charges. See [installation, timeouts, environment variables, and upgrade steps](docs/installation.md) for complete instructions and official client references.

## Controls that matter

- **Model constraints:** single-model mode locks provider/model/effort. Provider mode also locks model/effort unless the user enables caller overrides; the provider stays locked.
- **Execution evidence:** requested and effective model selections are separate. `effectiveSelection` is populated only after the bridge observes a request, and does not prove provider acceptance or billing.
- **Permissions:** new-session presets use Harness's official permission service; that selector leaves existing sessions unchanged. Full access is a high-risk option, not a setup requirement.
- **Task lifecycle:** start, wait, inspect, find, and cancel tasks. Client disconnects are separate from task cancellation; cancellation cannot undo completed effects.
- **Sessions:** continue bridge-managed conversations and archive/unarchive them. Automatic maintenance only archives; permanent deletion is unavailable.

The default connection uses a local pipe/socket with the stdio relay, without opening a TCP port. Optional HTTP is off by default. Update the plugin and the entire relay together; 0.2.4 uses `tls-pinned-v3` and does not fall back to older handshakes.

## Documentation

- [Installation and Claude Code / Codex setup](docs/installation.md)
- [Configuration, model defaults, and permission boundaries](docs/configuration.md)
- [Tool reference, task recovery, and session maintenance](docs/usage.md)
- [Troubleshooting and FAQ](docs/troubleshooting.md)
- [Delegating useful work](docs/delegation.md)
- [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [Security and responsible reporting](SECURITY.md)

## Permission boundaries

There are two separate decisions: whether your MCP client may call a bridge tool, and whether the Harness agent may perform an operation. Client-side MCP approval is not a replacement for Harness execution approval. Choosing a workspace does not by itself sandbox an agent.

Start in a disposable workspace with a small, read-only task. Keep credentials out of prompts, screenshots, and issue reports. Review substantive results before accepting changes. Back up important session data. Plugin deletion stays disabled until an official safe cross-process deletion boundary is available.

## Compatibility and verification

This bridge relies on version-specific Harness APIs and storage behavior. Other Harness versions, alternate profiles, and all client/platform combinations are not implied to be supported.

The repository includes maintainer-written technical records in Chinese: [reliability changes](docs/audit-2026-10-17.md), [desktop transport checks](docs/desktop-2026-10-18.md), and [new-session permission checks](docs/ui-permissions-2026-10-18.md). The [0.2.4 maintenance notes](docs/recheck-0.2.4.md) distinguish the current changes from earlier historical reports. Their stated test scope and remaining gaps matter; they are not a claim that all security risks or UI paths have been validated.

## Contribute

Bug reports, compatibility checks, translations, and focused pull requests are welcome in English or Chinese. Please read the [contribution guide](CONTRIBUTING.md), and keep secrets and private session content out of public reports.

If this project helps your workflow, a star helps others discover it.

## License

[MIT](LICENSE). The existing copyright and license notices apply.

# dsh-rea-toggle

[English](#english) · [中文](#中文)

One switch per conversation that decides whether the **REA**
(`reverse-engineer-anything`) MCP server's context reaches the model at all.

REA registers **207 tool schemas** plus a multi-kilobyte server-instructions
block. `dsh-mcp-client` puts both on the **global** layer, so every agent pays
for them on every request — whether or not the turn has anything to do with
reverse engineering.

With this plugin installed, a small pill appears below the composer:

- **REA on** (green) — exactly the pre-install behaviour. REA's tools and
  instructions are visible to the model.
- **REA off** (grey) — those 207 tool schemas and the `mcp:rea` instructions
  block **leave the model context**, taking effect on the next step.

**The switch is per conversation.** Each conversation remembers its own
position, and a new conversation starts **off**. That is the whole point: a
conversation about a web app should not pay for 207 reverse-engineering schemas
just because some other conversation needs them. Subagents inherit the position
of the conversation that created them, so delegating inside reverse-engineering
work does not silently break the subagent.

The same switch is on the keyboard: `/rea off`, `/rea on`, `/rea status`,
`/rea toggle` — all acting on the conversation you typed them in.

Nothing is uninstalled and nothing restarts. The MCP connection stays up; the
model simply stops being told those tools exist.

---

## English

### What it actually does

The token cost comes from two different places that travel two different paths,
so one mechanism is not enough:

| Target | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Tool schemas | `tools.restrict({ deny })` is called **in each agent's own context**. `ToolRuntime.view()` filters what that scope *inherits* from the global layer, and the model-facing schema list is rebuilt from that view on every assembly. The reserved `run_code` transport sits outside the filterable layers, so it is unaffected. |
| Instructions text | `dsh-mcp-client` registers the server instructions as a prompt section named `mcp:<server>` at order `MCP_SERVERS` (3100). **A scoped section with the same name shadows the global one** — a documented contract of `systemPrompt.section()` ("a scoped section shadows a global section with the same name"), not an implementation detail — and an empty section is dropped at render (`renderPrompt` keeps only `text.length > 0`). Registering that name and returning `''` therefore removes the block for that agent alone. |

Both are scoped registrations, so disposing them restores the previous state
exactly. That is why flipping the switch needs no restart and no reload.

Coverage includes **subagents**: `agent/created` is serial and awaited by the
registry, so installing inside it lands ahead of any prompt assembly.

### Install

```bash
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add github:aurumple/dsh-rea-toggle
```

Or point at a checkout:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add link:/absolute/path/to/dsh-rea-toggle
```

The bundle row id is `rea-toggle`; the package name is `dsh-rea-toggle`.

### Use

| Where | What |
| --- | --- |
| Pill under the composer | Click to flip **this conversation**. Green = on, grey = off, red border = the host did not answer. |
| `/rea off` · `/rea on` | Set this conversation's position. `enable` / `disable` work too. |
| `/rea toggle` | Flip this conversation. |
| `/rea status` | Report this conversation's position. |

A new conversation starts off. The first time you turn one on, that conversation
is remembered; conversations you never touch stay on the default and are not
written down.

Positions are remembered in `$DSH_HOME/rea-toggle.json` (usually
`~/.dsh/rea-toggle.json`), keyed by session id, and survive a restart. The file
keeps the 500 most recently changed conversations; an older one simply falls
back to the default.

### Configuration

Every field is optional.

```yaml
- id: rea-toggle
  name: dsh-rea-toggle
  config:
    server: rea               # one MCP server to govern; default "rea"
    # servers: [rea, ghidra]  # or several; wins over `server` when present
    # defaultEnabled: true    # new conversations start ON instead of off
```

Changing `server` governs a different MCP server by the same rules: tool prefix
`mcp__<server>__`, instructions section `mcp:<server>`. Because the mechanism is
generic, this works for any MCP server whose tools are bridged by
`dsh-mcp-client` — the REA case is just the one that motivated it.

`defaultEnabled` exists for anyone who wants the pre-plugin behaviour back: with
it on, a conversation nobody has switched behaves exactly as if this plugin were
not installed.

### HTTP API

The Client half talks to the Host over one exact route on the bare `webServer`
(the same shape other bundles use, so it does not travel through the `/api`
prefix fence). The conversation is `session=` on GET and a body field on POST:
the pill always knows which conversation it is showing, and a request that does
not say cannot be answered for it.

```
GET  /rea-toggle/state?session=<id>
  -> { session, enabled, known, defaultEnabled, servers, agents, tools, statePath }

GET  /rea-toggle/state            (no session: a summary)
  -> { session: null, defaultEnabled, servers, conversations, agents, tools, statePath }

POST /rea-toggle/state
  body: { "session": "<id>", "enabled": true | false }   (omit `enabled` to flip)
  -> the per-conversation status object
```

`known` says whether this conversation has ever been switched; when it is
`false`, `enabled` is just `defaultEnabled` and nothing has been written yet.
`agents` is how many live agents of that conversation are currently covered;
`tools` is how many of the governed server's tools were recognised, which is the
honest answer to "did it find REA at all" — if it reads `0`, the server is not
connected under that name (and stays `0`-safe because `restrictableNames` is the
denyable set, not the filtered view).

### Scope and limits

- **One server per row by default.** Other MCP servers are untouched; use
  `servers` to govern more than one.
- **Hidden, not unloaded.** The MCP connection stays up and the REA process
  keeps running. When the switch is off the model simply cannot reach it —
  including indirectly through `run_code`. That is deliberate: leaving a second
  path open would save only half the tokens.
- **Per-conversation state, in-process.** Positions are read from the file at
  `apply()` and written on every change. Two DSH instances sharing one profile
  each read it once and do not live-sync with each other.
- **It does not delete anything.** Turning it off is reversible in one click,
  and uninstalling the bundle lifts every registration.

### Verify it yourself

The claim is that the tools are gone from the model's context, not merely
hidden in a UI. Check it where the model's own view is exposed:

1. With the switch **on**, ask the agent to list its tools — `mcp__rea__*`
   entries are there (207 of them for a stock REA install).
2. Turn it **off**, ask again — they are gone, and calling one by name returns
   `Error: unknown tool "mcp__rea__binary_session"`.
3. Turn it back **on** — they return, unchanged.
4. Open a **second conversation** and check its tool list: it is off, while the
   first one is still on. That is the property that distinguishes this plugin
   from a global toggle.

### Development

```bash
npm test        # node:test, no dependencies
```

The suite drives the real `apply()` against a small model of the three
contracts it depends on (tool view, prompt section merge, agent registry). It
pins what "off" removes, that "on" restores the previous state exactly, that a
new subagent is covered before its first step, that the position survives a
restart, and that the HTTP surface validates its input.

### License

MIT

---

## 中文

一个开关（**每个对话一个**），决定 **REA**（`reverse-engineer-anything`）MCP
服务器的上下文是否进入模型。

REA 注册了 **207 个工具 schema**，外加一段几千字的服务端说明。
`dsh-mcp-client` 把它们放在**全局层**，所以每个 agent、每次请求都在为它们付
token —— 不管这一轮到底要不要逆向。

装上这个插件后，聊天输入框下方会多一个小胶囊：

- **REA 开**（绿色）— 和装之前完全一样，REA 的工具与说明对模型可见。
- **REA 关**（灰色）— 这 207 个工具 schema 和

plugins.readme_text:
DSH Mobile — DeepSeek Harness Remote

An open-source Android companion that puts your DeepSeek Harness in your pocket.
Drive sessions, review plans and goals, answer approvals and questions, and get notified when the harness finishes — from your phone, over your network or a relay.

English · 中文 · हिन्दी · Español · Français · ไทย

DSH Mobile is an **unofficial companion app** for the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (MIT). It mirrors the web GUI feature for feature and uses the harness's own visual language. Android only, Kotlin + Jetpack Compose. Its companion on the other end is [**dsh-relay**](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-relay), a harness plugin that adds the authentication layer the harness says it lacks, so this app can reach a harness with a real credential and a pinned key instead of an open port. See [Relay](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/wiki/Relay). **[dshm.zyphite.com](https://dshm.zyphite.com)** is the project site: what the app is, what it looks like, and how to get it running, on one page. The [**wiki**](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/wiki) is the user-facing guide: [getting started](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/wiki/Getting-Started), [connecting](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/wiki/Connecting), [troubleshooting](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/wiki/Troubleshooting), a [feature tour](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/wiki/Feature-Tour) and an [FAQ](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/wiki/FAQ). --- ## Screenshots | Connect | Chat | Trajectory | |:--:|:--:|:--:| | | | | | Recent harnesses with live reachability, LAN discovery, manual `host:port`, auto-connect. | Streamed turns, a glyph per tool, expandable tool cards, permission picker. | The same session as a per-turn ledger with usage totals. | | Session details | Subagents | |:--:|:--:| | | | | Context breakdown, goal, plan mode, background jobs, queued turns, host info, session-log export. | The subagent catalog — open a child's transcript, follow up, or interrupt it. | ## Features - Connecting — finds a harness on your Wi-Fi with an active subnet scan and a readiness handshake, remembers hosts and probes them for liveness on the way in, takes a manual `host:port`, handles loopback for same-device setups, and auto-connects when you tell it to (last used, LAN, or same device). - Navigation — the drawers work like Discord's: swipe right from the left edge for the workspace-grouped chat list, swipe left to close it, swipe left from the right edge for the session details panel. - Chat — streamed turns with reasoning disclosure, markdown, terminal/diff/read/search/web tool cards, a queue dock where you can edit, remove or steer a queued turn, history paging, and multi-photo and file attachments. Drafts are kept per host and session. - Workspace panels — tabbed text, Markdown, image, PDF and isolated HTML previews; native terminal controls with a bundled xterm renderer; archived-session restore in Settings. - Message feedback — confirmed ratings and retraction, with version-conflict handling. - Slash commands and skills — typing `/` lists the session's commands and skills above the composer. The composer checks a `/` line against the session's own command catalog and runs it through the harness's command gateway. Anything the catalog does not claim is sent as a prompt, which is how skills get invoked. With the dsh-rewind plugin on the host, `/rewind` opens a picker. - Everything the GUI does — goals (phases, rounds, pause/resume/edit), plan mode and plan review, permission approvals, user questions, todo dock, subagents (catalog, follow-ups, interrupt), background jobs, workflow runs, skills, model selection, agent presets, session search, trajectory ledger, session export, message feedback. - Notifications — turn complete, goal complete or blocked, review or question waiting for you. A foreground service keeps the connection alive in the background. - Harness look — the exact DeepSeek Harness design tokens (colors, type, radii, disclosure rows, shimmer, ink buttons), with light, dark and system themes. - 11 languages — English, 中文, हिन्दी, Español, Français, العربية, বাংলা, Português, Русский, اردو, ไทย (RTL aware). ### Added in 0.15.0 - A Check now button for updates in Settings > About. The automatic check also runs again when you come back to the app after a few hours. - Workspace links in replies drawn as file and folder pills; a folder opens in Files. - A redesigned Details panel, Workspace screen and Settings, with archived sessions on a tab of their own. ### Added in 0.14.0 - A `/` menu above the composer with the session's commands and skills. - A picker for the dsh-rewind plugin's `/rewind` and `/undo` that asks for confirmation before it restores files. The transcript hides what a rewind withdrew and marks the cut. ### Added in 0.13.0 - Automation catalog, timing edits, delivery history and session shortcuts. - Plugin installation, updates, toggles, removal, progress and recovery. Create plugin stages an unsent draft with the Creator preset when the host offers it. - Timed questions, continued replies, saved answer drafts and reopenable plans. - Draft text and file, folder and session references saved across app restarts. - Model search, YAML document properties and multiline goal editing. - Reverse-proxy path support and tool argument previews while the model is writing. ## Requirements - Android 8.0+ (minSdk 26). - A running [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) at `0.2.1-alpha.2`, the protocol baseline for DSH Mobile `0.16.0`. Existing protocol fallbacks remain for `0.2.0-rc.1`, `0.1.7-rc.x` and `0.1.6-alpha.x`; new management features need host support. See [compatibility](docs/COMPATIBILITY.md) and the [0.13.0 validation status](docs/VALIDATION-0.13.0.md) for what has been checked on this baseline. ## Quick start 1. Install the latest APK from [Releases](https://github.com/sorsama/deepseek-harness-mobile/releases/latest). 2. Open the app and choose how to connect.
